content: Adenovirus infections primarily affect the respiratory system, but depending on the serotype, they can also lead to other illnesses such as gastroenteritis, conjunctivitis, cystitis, and rash-related conditions. Individuals with compromised immune systems are particularly vulnerable to severe complications from adenovirus infections. Recent studies have identified certain adenoviruses, especially adenovirus 36 (AD-36), as a cause of obesity in animals and a potential contributor to human obesity. Acute respiratory disease (ARD), first identified among military recruits during World War II, can result from adenovirus infections under conditions of crowding and stress. Adenoviruses are transmitted through direct contact, fecal-oral routes, and occasionally via waterborne transmission. Some serotypes can establish persistent asymptomatic infections in the tonsils, adenoids, and intestines, with viral shedding occurring for months or even years. Serotypes 1, 2, 5, and 6 are endemic in certain regions and are typically acquired during childhood. Other serotypes cause sporadic infections or outbreaks, such as epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, which is associated with adenovirus serotypes 8, 19, and 37. Waterborne transmission of some adenovirus types, often linked to inadequately chlorinated swimming pools and small lakes, has been associated with febrile illnesses accompanied by conjunctivitis. In the United States, ARD is most commonly linked to adenovirus types 4 and 7, while enteric adenoviruses 40 and 41 are known to cause gastroenteritis, particularly in children. The clinical manifestations of adenovirus infections vary depending on the site of infection and the serotype. For instance, adenovirus 7 acquired through inhalation is associated with severe lower respiratory tract disease, whereas oral transmission of the same virus typically results in no or mild disease. Outbreaks of adenovirus-associated respiratory disease are more frequent in late winter, spring, and early summer, although infections can occur year-round. Common symptoms of adenovirus infections include the common cold syndrome, pneumonia, croup, and bronchitis. Laboratory diagnosis can be achieved through antigen detection, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, virus isolation, and serology. Adenovirus typing is typically performed using hemagglutination-inhibition or neutralization tests with type-specific antisera. It is important to note that the presence of adenovirus does not necessarily indicate active disease, as the virus can be excreted for prolonged periods. Most adenovirus infections are mild and require no specific therapy or only symptomatic treatment. Since there is no virus-specific treatment available, management of severe adenovirus illness focuses on addressing symptoms and complications. Deaths from adenovirus infections are exceedingly rare but have been reported. Prevention strategies include the use of safe and effective vaccines developed for adenovirus serotypes 4 and 7, which were previously available to prevent ARD among U.S. military recruits but ceased production in 1996. Strict adherence to infection-control practices is effective in preventing nosocomial outbreaks of adenovirus-associated diseases, such as epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Maintaining adequate levels of chlorination in swimming pools is essential to prevent outbreaks of adenovirus conjunctivitis associated with waterborne transmission.
